title: The hypertrophy series: How to balance mentally taxing exercises in your training
summary: He explains mental fatigue as a recovery factor: some lifts (for him the squat) spike stress and drain confidence, while total volume also drains focus. Within a session, start with the stressful compound but avoid a declining 'staircase' that makes you skip late isolation work; place stress 'spikes' later to stay engaged. Across the week, never stack mentally taxing days back to back, and use prioritization to decide which big lift gets the emphasis.

claims.claim: Mental fatigue is an aspect of recovery people ignore; a lift affects your mind as well as your body.
A lift you approach with confidence barely spikes stress or cortisol, while a lift you are uncomfortable with or keep failing can shatter your confidence and be hard to recover from.
Don't simply drop lifts that stress you; the lifts that stress you are the ones that challenge and change you most.
The squat is currently his most stressful lift because of nagging issues that reflect a glaring weak spot he needs to work on, so dropping it would cost him gains.
Think of a session as a mental stamina economy: put the most mentally taxing exercise, usually the heavy compound strength work, at the very start.
If your main lift doesn't tax you mentally, you can add a second taxing lift in the same session; bench doesn't stress him, so he pairs it with overhead press on the same day.
High training volume also drains you mentally: at the end of long sessions the body may still be fresh while the brain is foggy and unfocused.

A natural bodybuilder can push work capacity so high that the limit becomes the brain's ability to drive the body rather than the body itself, and a burnt-out brain prevents reaching the extra stimulus needed to grow.
A very stressful exercise should be followed by less stressful ones.

The standard 'staircase' order (compound, variation, accessory, cable isolation) makes you complacent as the session goes on, because you put what you care about at the top and what you care less about at the bottom.
People attach self-worth to mentally taxing lifts and pour adrenaline into them, which makes everything after feel unimportant; as a bodybuilder every exercise should be equally important.
Most people skip isolation work at the end of the workout far more often than compounds, telling themselves the heavy stuff was enough; that is the wrong mindset.

Structure a session as spikes rather than a staircase: start high, drop to recover, then include another stress spike later, such as a favourite but demanding exercise placed late so you must get through the rest to reach it.
Across the week, don't put several highly mentally draining days in a row or you will underperform, get injured or burn out; the second day always suffers.

Even with a day between, a very stressful Monday makes a stressful Wednesday less effective, creating a dilemma with heavy lower-body compounds where the first session of the week is best and later ones suffer.
He puts his lower-body days on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, rests Sunday after the heavy Saturday lower day, and has a fresh Monday, shrinking the window of mentally taxing work.
How to manage mental fatigue depends on your split and must be learned by applying it yourself; you can't learn it from books or copy it from him.

Prioritization resolves conflicts: his quads are big enough to just maintain while he wants bigger hamstrings, so he prioritizes deadlifts over squats and goes lighter on squats since both are highly taxing.
Managing mentally taxing lifts matters more once you're advanced and train more often, but it is present for everyone and awareness beats training blind.
